```{r, include = FALSE}
source("../setup.R")
docs_setup(legend = "right")
options(warn = 1)
```

A lit surface shows its orientation through brightness. When fill represents
data, its legend needs to account for the colour changes caused by lighting.
This article lights a height surface and uses shaded colour guides to read it.
Installation is covered in [Get started](ggplot3d.html); the multi-panel
examples use patchwork to arrange the views. [Styling axes, legends and panes](guides-themes.html) covers guide placement and panel furniture.

```{r setup}
library(ggplot3d)
library(ggplot2)
d <- expand.grid(x = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 36), y = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 36))
d$z <- with(d, exp(-(x^2 + y^2)) + 0.5 * exp(-((x - 1)^2 + (y + 1)^2) * 2))
hill <- ggplot(d, aes(x, y, z = z, fill = z)) +
  geom_surface_3d(shading = "smooth", colour = NA)
```

## Colour that survives shading

By default the light moves only the OKLab lightness of the fill and keeps
its hue: faces turned toward the light get lighter, faces turned away get
darker, and a face at the `neutral` angle to the light keeps its colour
exactly, so the colour stays recognisable against its key.

```{r lightness, fig.alt="A two-peaked surface coloured by height, with a colourbar showing each colour's shading range."}
hill + scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Spectral",
    guide = guide_colourbar_3d(along = NULL, shading_range = TRUE)) +
  coord_3d()
```

The colourbar now shows each value from shadow (left) to full light
(right), sampled from the same shading kernel as the faces. A palette that
changes lightness with value, such as viridis, loses the most under
shading, since shading changes lightness too; a diverging or isoluminant
palette leaves lightness free for the shape.

`light_3d(mode = "multiply")` scales the fill by the light instead, as
matplotlib and rgl do. It can only darken, so a face at a grazing angle is a
darker version of its colour and a dark yellow no longer looks like the
yellow in the legend; and since the default light comes from near the
viewer, the faces that face the camera all get nearly the same light and
blend together.

`"tone"` moves the colour toward a shadow and a highlight colour instead,
and `"overlay"` and `"soft"` are the blend modes of matplotlib's
`LightSource`.

```{r tone, fig.alt="A height surface shaded toward blue shadows and warm highlights, with a stepped colour guide."}
hill + scale_fill_viridis_b(guide = guide_coloursteps_3d()) +
  coord_3d(light = light_3d(light_directional_3d(), mode = "tone",
    shadow_colour = "#22305a", highlight_colour = "#fff3d0"))
```

## Lighting presets

`light_3d(preset = )` starts from a ready-made lighting. `"contrast"` moves
the HSV value of the fill toward black or white, with a light from the side;
`"shade"` only darkens, by up to 70 percent, from a low light; `"headlight"`
lights from the eye and puts a white highlight where the surface turns
toward it; `"soft"` lights from above the viewer with a strong ambient term;
and `"studio"` tints the surface with four coloured lights, which suits
light fills. Apart from the default, each reproduces the surface lighting of
a widely used 3D package, named on the `light_3d()` help page. Any argument
given with a preset replaces the preset's value.

```{r presets, fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 5, fig.alt="Six copies of a blue surface with two peaks under the default, contrast, shade, headlight and soft lighting and, on a light grey fill, the studio lighting."}
presets <- c("default", "contrast", "shade", "headlight", "soft", "studio")
panels <- lapply(presets, function(preset) {
  ggplot(d, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
    geom_surface_3d(fill = if (preset == "studio") "grey85" else "#2E6F9E",
                    shading = "smooth", colour = NA) +
    coord_3d(light = light_3d(preset = preset), panes = character(),
             axes = character(), box = "none") +
    ggtitle(preset)
})
patchwork::wrap_plots(panels, ncol = 3)
```

A highlight mixes white into the fill to indicate surface orientation.
`material_3d("satin")` keeps it faint, and
`light_3d(material = )` gives every shaded layer without its own material
that one.

## Mesh lines, outlines and transparency

Shading shows the shape of a surface, and lines drawn on it show where its
grid runs and where it ends. `edges_3d()` draws the edges of the grid cells
over the faces, without the diagonals that split each cell into triangles;
`every` keeps every n-th line of a dense grid. `outline_3d()` draws feature
lines, among them the boundary of an open surface. Both are lines of the
scene, hidden by nearer parts of the surface, and both work with any
lighting. Given to `coord_3d()`, they apply to every surface layer that sets
none of its own, so one setting gives a whole figure its style; a layer
that sets `edges = FALSE` or `outline = FALSE` draws none.

Thin white lines with some transparency trace the grid over a dark fill.
Dark lines every few cells with a black boundary give a light fill the look
of a printed figure. A translucent fill (`alpha`) lets the far side of the
surface show through, and the lines on it show which part is in front.

```{r lines, fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 3.2, fig.alt="Three copies of the two-peaked surface: blue with a thin white grid, light grey under tinted lights with a dark grid every third line and a black boundary, and translucent blue with a white grid and a dark boundary."}
boundary <- outline_3d(silhouette = FALSE, crease = NULL)
lines <- function(title, fill, ...) {
  ggplot(d, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
    geom_surface_3d(fill = fill, shading = "smooth", ...) +
    ggtitle(title)
}
plain <- function(...) coord_3d(panes = character(), axes = character(), box = "none", ...)
patchwork::wrap_plots(
  lines("grid", "#2E6F9E") + plain(edges = edges_3d()),
  lines("every third line", "grey85") +
    plain(light = light_3d(preset = "studio"), outline = boundary,
          edges = edges_3d(every = 3, colour = "grey15", alpha = 1, linewidth = 0.15)),
  lines("translucent", "#2E6F9E", alpha = 0.6) +
    plain(edges = edges_3d(), outline = outline_3d(silhouette = FALSE, crease = NULL, colour = "#16384f")),
  nrow = 1)
```

## Illustrative styles

`material_3d(style = )` changes how a face responds to the light. Toon
shading quantises the response into bands, Gooch shading (Gooch et al.
1998) turns brightness into a cool-to-warm hue shift that keeps dark
regions readable, and normal colouring encodes the orientation of each face
as a colour.

```{r styles, fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 3.2, fig.alt="Three copies of the surface with toon bands, cool-to-warm Gooch shading and colours encoding face normals."}
plain <- ggplot(d, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  coord_3d(panes = character(), axes = character(), box = "none")
toon <- plain + geom_surface_3d(fill = "tomato", colour = NA,
  material = material_3d(style = "toon", bands = 4)) + ggtitle("toon")
gooch <- plain + geom_surface_3d(fill = "grey60", colour = NA, shading = "smooth",
  material = material_3d(style = "gooch")) + ggtitle("gooch")
normals <- plain + geom_surface_3d(colour = NA, shading = "smooth",
  material = material_3d(style = "normals")) + ggtitle("normals")
patchwork::wrap_plots(toon, gooch, normals, nrow = 1)
```

## Line drawings

`hatch_3d()` draws the tone as hatching. The strokes are cut from the
surface by parallel planes, so they follow it in depth and are hidden by
nearer parts like any other line; darker faces keep more of them. With a
white fill, feature lines from `outline_3d()` and the plotter backend, which
draws strokes only, the figure is a line drawing that an SVG device writes
for a pen plotter.

```{r hatch, fig.alt="The two-peaked surface drawn with outlines and hatching whose density varies with the light."}
ggplot(d, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_surface_3d(fill = "white", colour = NA, hatch = hatch_3d(angle = 0, spacing = 0.02),
    outline = outline_3d(linewidth = 0.4)) +
  coord_3d(backend = backend_3d("plotter"), panes = character(), box = "none")
```

## Light sources, shadows and depth

`light_3d()` combines one or more lights. `light_directional_3d()` shines from a direction, `light_point_3d()` from a position in the data with intensity falling off with distance, `light_head_3d()` from the camera, and `light_hemisphere_3d()` blends a sky colour from above with a ground colour from below. A point light just above one corner brightens the faces near it.

```{r point-light, fig.alt="A grey surface lit by a point light above one corner, brightest on the nearby slope."}
plain <- ggplot(d, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_surface_3d(fill = "grey80", colour = NA, shading = "smooth")
plain + coord_3d(light = light_3d(light_point_3d(c(-2, -2, 1.5), falloff = 1),
                                  light_hemisphere_3d(sky = "white", ground = "grey40")))
```

`shadow_3d()` casts the shadow of the scene onto the floor of the box from a directional light. Raising the lower z limit leaves room for the shadow below the surface.

```{r shadow, fig.alt="A surface with two peaks casting a dark shadow onto the floor of the box."}
plain + coord_3d(zlim = c(-0.5, 1.2),
  shadow = shadow_3d(light = light_3d(light_directional_3d(c(1, 1, 3), space = "data"))))
```

`depth_cue_3d()` makes depth readable without lighting: fog fades distant marks toward the background, `linewidth = TRUE` thins distant lines, and eye-dome lighting (`edl`) darkens the edges where depth jumps, which helps point clouds.

```{r depth-cue, fig.alt="A cube of points that fade toward grey with distance from the camera."}
lattice <- expand.grid(x = 1:6, y = 1:6, z = 1:6)
ggplot(lattice, aes(x, y, z = z)) + geom_point_3d(size = 2, colour = "#2E6F9E") +
  coord_3d(depth_cue = depth_cue_3d(fog = "grey90", amount = 0.8))
```

## Legends that show the shading

A colour key shows the fill before lighting, while the plot shows it after. `guide_colourbar_3d()`, `guide_coloursteps_3d()`, `guide_legend_3d()` and `guide_bins_3d()` add the range of shades that the light produces for each colour, so the darkest face in the plot can be matched to its key.

```{r guide-legend, fig.alt="Columns in four colours with a legend whose keys each show a band from shadowed to lit."}
columns <- expand.grid(x = 1:4, y = 1:2)
columns$z <- columns$x + columns$y
ggplot(columns, aes(x, y, z = z, fill = factor(x))) + geom_col_3d() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#2E6F9E", "#B5342B", "#3F7A3D", "#9E5E0F"),
                    name = "x") +
  guides(fill = guide_legend_3d(shading_range = TRUE)) + coord_3d()
```
